true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Second `self.downsize` definition silently replaces the width/height variant

`OptimizedImage.downsize` is defined twice: `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and `(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. Ruby keeps only the last definition, so the width/height signature no longer exists.

Every existing caller using `downsize(from, to, w, h, opts)` now fails:
- With five arguments it raises `ArgumentError`.
- With four arguments, `max_height` (an Integer) is bound to `opts`, and `opts[:force_aspect_ratio]` raises a `TypeError`.

This breaks existing downsizing (e.g. avatar and thumbnail code paths). Give the new method a distinct name, or have a single method that accepts both forms.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side size limit hardcoded to 10MB for all upload types, ignoring site settings

`validateUploadedFile` now uses a fixed 10MB limit instead of `max_<type>_size_kb`. That limit is only meant to let oversized images through for server-side downsizing, but it also applies to attachments.

Consequences:
- Attachments larger than `max_attachment_size_kb` pass client validation, upload fully, and are only rejected by the server.
- Sites configured with limits above 10MB can no longer upload files the server would accept.

The same hardcoding at line 246 makes the 413 error message report 10MB regardless of the real limit. Keep the setting-based limit for attachments, and only relax it for images.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated GIF downsizing passes a percentage to gifsicle, which it cannot use

When `allow_animated_thumbnails` is on and the file is a `.gif`, `optimize` routes to `resize_instructions_animated`, which runs `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. `--resize-fit` expects WxH dimensions, not a percentage.

As a result:
- gifsicle exits non-zero.
- `downsize` returns false, and the result is ignored.
- The loop burns all 5 attempts doing nothing.
- The oversized GIF is passed on unchanged and then rejected.

Animated GIFs, often the largest images, are never reduced.

true_positives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
In-place rewrite of tempfile path may leave the open Tempfile handle stale

The loop rewrites the file at `tempfile.path` in place. `convert` writes there, and `ImageOptim#optimize_image!` replaces the file, typically by writing a new file and renaming it over the path. The open `Tempfile` IO can still refer to the original inode.

If so:
- `tempfile.size` keeps reporting the original size, so the loop always runs the full 5 iterations of expensive conversions.
- `Upload.create_for(current_user.id, tempfile, ..., tempfile.size)` may read the original, unreduced content and size.

Also, the return value of `downsize` is ignored, so a failed conversion keeps looping. Re-open the file or use `File.size(tempfile.path)`, and stop when `downsize` returns false.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new automatic downsizing path or the `downsize` signature change

The PR adds the server-side downsize loop and changes the `OptimizedImage.downsize`/`optimize` signatures without adding any specs. A spec covering the old `downsize(from, to, w, h)` callers would have caught the method-redefinition breakage. A spec for oversized image uploads, including GIFs, would have caught the gifsicle issue.

URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB regardless of upload type or settings

API URL uploads are now capped at a fixed 10MB instead of following site settings. Two effects:
- Admins who raised `max_image_size_kb` or `max_attachment_size_kb` above 10MB can no longer upload such files by URL.
- Attachments up to 10MB are downloaded even when the configured attachment limit is far smaller, wasting bandwidth before the inevitable rejection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation raises on nil host

`self.host.sub!` is called unconditionally. When the host is nil, e.g. a POST or PUT to the admin endpoint without `embeddable_host[:host]`, this raises NoMethodError and returns a 500 instead of a validation error. Guard with `if host.present?` or use `self.host = host.to_s.sub(...)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy with unknown id raise NoMethodError

`EmbeddableHost.where(id: ...).first` returns nil for a missing id. `host.destroy` and `save_host(nil)` then raise NoMethodError and return a 500 instead of a 404. Use `find` or `raise Discourse::NotFound`.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Host lookup is not truly case-insensitive and ignores ports

The column is lowercased with `lower(host)`, but the parameter is passed as-is from `uri.host`. Ruby's URI does not downcase hosts, so a referer like `http://EvilTrout.com` won't match. The validation regex also allows a `:port` suffix, but `uri.host` excludes the port, so a host saved with a port can never match. Downcase the parameter and either reject ports or compare them.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migrated hosts are not normalized and the raw value is interpolated into SQL

The old `embeddable_hosts` values are inserted verbatim, e.g. `http://eviltrout.com`, `https://example.com/1234`, or values with a trailing `\r` or whitespace. The old matcher stripped schemes and parsed URIs. The new `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares `lower(host)` to the bare `uri.host`, so these rows never match and embedding silently breaks for existing sites after upgrade. The value is also string-interpolated into the INSERT, so any quote in it breaks the migration. Strip scheme, path and whitespace, skip blank lines, and use `quote`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migrated hosts are not normalized and the raw value is interpolated into SQL

The old `embeddable_hosts` values are inserted verbatim, e.g. `http://eviltrout.com`, `https://example.com/1234`, or values with a trailing `\r` or whitespace. The old matcher stripped schemes and parsed URIs. The new `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares `lower(host)` to the bare `uri.host`, so these rows never match and embedding silently breaks for existing sites after upgrade. The value is also string-interpolated into the INSERT, so any quote in it breaks the migration. Strip scheme, path and whitespace, skip blank lines, and use `quote`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when embed_category is unset or doesn't match a category

The query joins `site_settings` to `categories` on the `embed_category` setting value and then calls `[0]['id']` on the result. If no `embed_category` row exists (the default case, since it defaulted to ''), or its value matches no category name, the result set is empty. `[0]` then returns nil and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError. The migration aborts on most installs, and the `category_id == 0` fallback is never reached. Check `cmd_tuples` or `ntuples` before indexing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.

false_positives.candidate:
"is false if embeddable_host is blank" no longer tests what it says

`expandable_first_post?` no longer depends on embeddable hosts. This test passes only because `embed_truncate` defaults to false. The test name is misleading, and the outer `before` block that `Fabricate`s a host has no effect on the behavior under test.

Delete failures are silently swallowed

`destroyRecord()` has no `.catch(popupAjaxError)`. If the server delete fails, the admin gets no feedback and the promise rejection is unhandled. The save action does handle errors, so delete is inconsistent with it.

Test requests fruit 2 but the fixture always returns fruit 1

The pretender handler for `/fruits/:id` always returns `fruits[0]`, the apple with `color_ids [1,2]`. The test asks for fruit 2, the banana with `color_ids [3]`, yet asserts two colors with ids 1 and 2. It passes only because the id is ignored, so it misrepresents what is being tested and would fail if the fixture honored the id.

type.replace('_','-') only replaces the first underscore

`String#replace` with a string pattern replaces only the first occurrence. Any admin model type with two or more underscores won't be normalized and will be routed to `/` instead of `/admin/`. Use `/_/g`.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unsubscribe crashes with NoMethodError when no TopicUser row exists

`TopicUser.find_by(user_id:, topic_id:)` returns nil when the user has no topic_users row for the topic. That happens, for example, to a user who was mentioned or quoted in a topic they never visited. The next line calls `tu.notification_level` on nil, so clicking the email unsubscribe link raises NoMethodError and returns a 500. Use `TopicUser.change`, which creates the row if needed, or handle the nil case explicitly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new unsubscribe endpoint

The new `TopicsController#unsubscribe` action has no controller specs. Untested cases include the level transitions (watching/tracking to regular, regular to muted), the missing-TopicUser case, the slug redirect, and the logged-out behavior. The only spec change adds an `unsubscribe_url` argument to an existing MessageBuilder test and does not assert that the link appears.

State-changing unsubscribe exposed as a GET with no CSRF protection, and it toggles on repeat The unsubscribe action changes the user's notification level on a plain GET. Any third-party page can embed `` and change a logged-in user's settings. Email link scanners, prefetchers and page reloads also trigger it. The action is not idempotent: the first hit drops watching/tracking to regular, and a second hit (a refresh or revisit) drops regular to muted. The user ends up muted without intending it. Have the GET render a confirmation page and perform the change via POST/PUT, or use a signed per-user token.

save! bypasses TopicUser.change, so the level can be silently reverted and clients are not notified

The level is written with `tu.save!` instead of `TopicUser.change`. As a result `notifications_reason_id` and `notifications_changed_at` are not set, and no MessageBus `notification_level_change` is published to the user's open clients. When `notifications_reason_id` is still NULL, `update_last_read` auto-promotes the row back to `tracking` once read time exceeds the auto-track threshold. A user who unsubscribed can therefore be re-subscribed just by reading the topic. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)`.

unsubscribe_link now needs %{unsubscribe_url}; senders that don't pass it break

The shared `unsubscribe_link` string now interpolates `%{unsubscribe_url}`. `MessageBuilder#body` and `#html_part` render it for every email built with `add_unsubscribe_link: true`. Only `send_notification_email` was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url`. Any other sender that sets `add_unsubscribe_link` without it will raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument or render a broken link. Even when the URL is present, the per-topic sentence is wrong for emails that are not about a single topic. Use a separate translation key, or only add the topic sentence when `unsubscribe_url` is present.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Validation side effect counts each signup attempt twice

`EmailValidator` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, which writes to the database (match_count, last_match_at) on every validation. `UsersController#create` runs `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which validates again. Every signup attempt with a matching email therefore increments match_count by 2, making the statistics wrong. More generally, any extra `valid?` call anywhere inflates the counts. Recording the match should be moved out of the validator, or done only once per attempt.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and trivially bypassed

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` does an exact, case-sensitive match on PostgreSQL, and neither the stored value nor the incoming value is normalized (e.g. with `Email.downcase`/strip). If `bad@spammers.org` is blocked, signing up as `Bad@Spammers.org` passes the block check. Both sides should be normalized to lowercase before comparing or storing. The uniqueness validation and the unique index on `blocked_emails.email` have the same case gap, so duplicates differing only by case can be inserted.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Match statistics recorded inside the user save transaction are rolled back on failure

Because `should_block?` saves the BlockedEmail record during the User's validation, the write happens inside the User save transaction. In `save!`/`create_for_email`, a blocked email raises RecordInvalid and the transaction rolls back, losing the match_count/last_match_at update. Statistics are then inconsistent depending on the call path (`save` vs `save!`).

rejectedEmails array is defined on the prototype and shared/persistent

`rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` in `extend()` creates one array shared by every instance of the controller, and it is never cleared. If an email is rejected for a transient reason (for example 'has already been taken' because of a race), it stays rejected client-side for the rest of the page session. The array should be initialized per instance in `init` and reset when the modal is reopened.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Substring-based origin check for postMessage

`discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1` accepts any origin that is a substring of discourseUrl. For example, `https://forum.example.co` passes the check for `https://forum.example.com/`. The origin should be compared exactly against the parsed origin of discourseUrl.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: URL interpolated unescaped into HTML attribute `#{url}` builds raw HTML from the feed item's link/id without escaping. That HTML is then rendered unsanitized via the raw_html cook method. A URL containing a `'` breaks out of the href attribute and lets an attacker inject arbitrary markup or event handlers. `url` should be HTML-escaped (e.g. `ERB::Util.html_escape`).

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end if` typo turns following template output into the if-modifier condition

`<%- end if %>` compiles to `end if` followed by the next generated `@output_buffer.safe_append=...` statement. Ruby parses that statement as the modifier condition, so the template only works by accident because the append is truthy and evaluated first, which reorders output. It should be `<%- end %>`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Crash on feed items without content / on Ruby < 2.1

`i.content.scrub` assumes every item has a `content` element. Many RSS feeds only provide `description`, so `content` is nil and the call raises NoMethodError, aborting the whole poll. Because `retry: false` is set, nothing after that item is imported. `String#scrub` also only exists in Ruby 2.1+, so on Ruby 2.0 this raises for every item. A fallback to `description` and a nil guard are needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Editing an existing migration to add force: true

Adding `force: true` to an already-shipped migration does nothing on installs that have already run it. On re-runs it silently drops the existing `top_topics` table. Changing historical migrations is unrelated to this feature and risky.

Every new embed URL triggers a full synchronous feed poll

`perform_retrieve` calls `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline whenever an embed URL is unknown. That fetches the whole feed over HTTP and runs import, including SHA comparisons and possible revisions, for every item. The only throttle is per URL. Any visitor hitting distinct article URLs (or the same URL with different query strings) on the embeddable host forces repeated full feed downloads and imports. There is no caching of the feed fetch (`feed_key` is defined but never used).

Nil post when embed's post was deleted

`post = embed.post` can be nil if the post was hard-deleted, or not found because it was trashed via the default scope. `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!` then raises NoMethodError on every feed poll for that URL, breaking the import of all subsequent items.

Protocol-relative URLs are mangled by absolutize_urls

Any href or src starting with '/' is treated as host-relative, including protocol-relative URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.png`. The leading slashes are stripped and the embed host is prepended, producing `http://host/cdn.example.com/img.png`. This breaks every protocol-relative link and image in imported content. Values starting with '//' should be skipped or resolved properly, e.g. with `URI.join`.

Unsanitized feed/remote HTML stored as raw_html post (stored XSS)

Content from the RSS/Atom feed (`PollFeed`) or from a remote page (`import_remote`) is saved with `cook_method: raw_html`. `Post#cook` then returns `raw` as-is, with no sanitizer. The embed view outputs it with `raw post.cooked`, and the normal Discourse topic view renders it too. Any `<script>`, `onerror=` or `javascript:` content in the feed therefore runs on the forum origin. A compromised or malicious feed, or a hijacked page on the embeddable host, gets full XSS against forum users, including admins. The HTML should be sanitized with a whitelist before it is stored.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin emits a nonexistent property and passes unmapped values to the old syntax

`-ms-align-items` is not a real property; IE10 uses `-ms-flex-align`. The mixin also passes `$alignment` unchanged to `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`. Those properties only accept `start`/`end`/`center`/`baseline`/`stretch`, so any future call with `flex-start` or `flex-end` silently fails on the prefixed syntaxes. Remove the bogus property and map `flex-start`/`flex-end` to `start`/`end`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Header panel alignment relies on auto margins unsupported by the legacy -webkit-box fallback

`float: right` on `.panel` was replaced by `margin-left: auto`. The new `flexbox()` mixin deliberately emits `display: -webkit-box` / `-moz-box` for old browsers. The 2009 box model does not distribute auto margins, so in those browsers the panel (search, hamburger, user icons) is no longer pushed to the right. It ends up packed next to the title, which is a regression from the previous float layout. Either drop the legacy fallbacks or add a legacy-compatible way to push the panel right, such as `-webkit-box-flex` on the title or `-webkit-box-pack: justify`.

small-action button no longer floats right after container became flex

This PR makes `.small-action` a flex container (`@include flexbox()`). In a flex container, `float` on children is ignored, so `float: right` on the `button` rule no longer works. Nothing replaces it: there is no `margin-left: auto` and no `justify-content`. As a result, the edit/delete button in small-action posts now sits immediately after the description text instead of at the right edge. Add `margin-left: auto` to the button. `float: left` on `.topic-avatar` and `clear: both` are also dead code now.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name lacks `?`, so website_name leaks for TL0 users seen by anonymous viewers

ActiveModel::Serializers only honours filter methods named `include_<attr>?`. The method here is `include_website_name` with no question mark, so it is never consulted and `website_name` is always serialized.

On top of that, `website_name` is not listed in `untrusted_attributes`. For a TL0 user viewed anonymously, `website` is hidden by `restrict_user_fields?`, but `website_name` still exposes the website host and, for same-domain sites, the full path. That defeats the anti-spam restriction on untrusted profile fields.

Fix: rename the method to `include_website_name?` and make it apply the same `restrict_user_fields?` check, e.g. by adding `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes`.

false_positives.candidate:
Sibling-subdomain heuristic treats unrelated domains under multi-part TLDs as the same site

The sibling branch decides two hosts belong to the same site by stripping only the first label from each and comparing the rest. Unrelated sites under multi-part public suffixes therefore match: `foo.co.uk` vs `bar.co.uk` compares `co.uk == co.uk` and shows the full URL path. Likewise `a.github.io` vs `b.github.io` would match.

The display is then inconsistent with the intent of only showing the full path for the instance's own domain.

Untrusted-attribute spec does not cover the new website_name field

The TL0/anonymous spec checks that untrusted attributes are absent, but its list does not include `website_name`. As a result, the leak of the website host and path to anonymous viewers goes untested.

The new specs also never exercise the sibling-subdomain branch (www.example.com vs forum.example.com) or the `website_host.nil?` path.

true_positives.golden_comment: In .topic-meta-data h5 a, the original code had color: scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%) but was changed to dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%)). The lightness for the light theme changed from 30% to 70%, which is a dramatic inversion
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Embedded post author link colour flipped from 30% to 70% lightness in light themes

The original rule was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. Every other conversion in this PR keeps the original value for light themes and uses the complement for dark ones. Here the arguments are swapped: `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%))`. As a result, `.embedded-posts .topic-meta-data h5 a` becomes much paler in light themes. It should be `(…$primary 30%, …$secondary 70%)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: This change for desktop/user.css changes $primary from 30% to 50% for the light theme; most other changes preserve the original $primary value and move the complement to $secondary for dark. Consider reviewing this (also applies to a similar .name change in the mobile variant).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
group-member-info .name light-theme lightness changed from 30% to 50%

The original rule was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The replacement uses 50%/50%, which lightens member names in light themes. This is an unintended visual regression. It should be `(…$primary 30%, …$secondary 70%)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In topic-post.css the original code used $lightness: 70% but the replacement uses $lightness: 30% for the light theme. This makes the text significantly darker than intended.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
custom-message-length colour inverted for light themes

The original rule was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`. The new rule uses `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)` for light themes and `$secondary 70%` for dark. The values were swapped, so this hint text becomes much darker on mobile light themes. The desktop version keeps 70%/30%. It should be `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 30%))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The light theme color for `.topic-meta-data h5 a` was changed from `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)` to `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)`, which may unintentionally reduce contrast and affect readability. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with design intentions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

false_positives.candidate:
Breaking change to admin groups API without compatibility

`create` and `update` now read flat params (`params[:name]`) instead of the nested `params[:group][...]`. Membership via `usernames` on create/update and the PATCH `changes: {add:, delete:}` interface were removed. Existing API consumers will silently lose updates: nested params are ignored, `visible` is reset to false because `params[:visible]` is nil, and their membership changes no longer apply. The removed `get "users"` route also breaks any caller using it. This should be documented or kept backward compatible.

Public members endpoint accepts unbounded/negative limit and offset

`limit` and `offset` come straight from params with no clamping on this non-admin endpoint. Anyone who can see a group can pass `limit=10000000` and force loading and serializing every member of a huge automatic group (e.g. trust_level_0). A negative `limit` or `offset` reaches Postgres, which rejects a negative OFFSET or LIMIT and returns a 500. Clamp `limit` to a sane maximum (e.g. 1..200) and `offset` to >= 0.

addMembers/removeMember have no error handling

Neither the model nor the controller actions handle rejection. If the server returns 422, for example for an automatic group, the error is swallowed and the admin gets no feedback. The added usernames also stay in the input; the TODO acknowledges this.

create ignores alias_level sent by the form

The new form shows the alias level combo-box when creating a group, and `asJSON` sends `alias_level`, but `create` only sets `name` and `visible`. Any alias level chosen at creation is silently discarded until the group is saved again.

remove_member bypasses Group#remove and model callbacks

The previous code removed members via `group.remove(user)`. The new code uses `group.users.delete(user_id)`, and on a has_many :through association this defaults to a delete_all strategy that skips GroupUser destroy callbacks. Any cleanup tied to leaving a group can be silently skipped, such as clearing the user's primary_group or title, or keeping user_count in sync. If the user is not a member, `find` raises RecordNotFound, producing a 404 rather than a clean error. Use `group.remove(user)` with an explicit user lookup.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded in the web request path, not in jobs or mailers

With the accelerator patch, translations load on demand. `I18n.translate` only loads `config.locale`, and the fallback locales (site default and `:en`) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`. That call happens solely in `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks and other non-controller code never call it. In those contexts the Fallbacks backend looks up keys in locales that were never loaded and gets nil, so fallbacks silently do not work and users see 'translation missing' text. The fallback locales should be loaded inside `I18n.translate`/`load_locale`, not in a controller filter.

No tests for new fallback behavior

The PR changes translation resolution for every locale but adds no specs. Untested cases include: fallback to the site locale then to English, loading of the fallback locales, and behavior in non-request contexts. Regressions such as the missing-load issue in jobs would go unnoticed.

SiteSetting lookup on every fallback resolution

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds a new array and reads `SiteSetting.default_locale` on every call. The Fallbacks backend calls it on every uncached translate, which includes every translate call that has interpolation or count arguments, since those bypass the LRU cache. This allocates a new array on every one of those calls and adds avoidable overhead to a very hot path.

Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, so stale or missing results stay cached

Results now depend on the fallback chain: `SiteSetting.default_locale`, plus which fallback locales happen to be loaded. The LRU cache key is still only key + `config.locale` + backend id. Two problems follow. (1) If the site's default locale changes, cached fallback strings from the old default locale keep being served until the process restarts or the entry is evicted. (2) If a key is translated before the fallback locales are loaded (e.g. outside a controller), the 'translation missing' result is frozen into the cache. It is then returned even after the fallback locales are loaded. The cache key should include the fallback chain, or the cache should be cleared when the default locale changes.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Conditional passkeys UI now only rendered when a user is already set, disabling it for normal login

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative QuerySet slicing is unsupported in Django and raises an error

The "advanced" branch slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. The comment claims the ORM handles negative slicing automatically, but it does not: Django raises `ValueError`/`AssertionError` ("Negative indexing is not supported").

A user-supplied cursor like `0:-5:0` therefore produces a 500 instead of a clean 400 `BadPaginationError`.

The comments also say this "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" and is "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level". That rationale is misleading. Negative offsets should be rejected, as `OffsetPaginator` does.

true_positives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Gate uses is_superuser rather than active superuser, and member may be None

`request.user.is_superuser` is true for superuser accounts even without an active superuser session. Sentry normally gates superuser-only behavior with `is_active_superuser(request)`, so this bypasses that convention.

Separately, for a non-superuser accessing via staff or other paths, `organization_context.member` can be `None`. In that case `.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError` and the request returns a 500.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator applies math.floor/ceil to datetime keys and crashes the audit log endpoint

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` copies the integer `Paginator` implementation and runs `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `getattr(item, self.key)`.

The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, uses `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime`. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`.

`build_cursor` calls `key(results[0])` whenever the page has results. So every `optimized_pagination=true` request that returns at least one row fails with a 500.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator change silently clamps negative next offsets but passes negative prev offsets to the QuerySet

This change affects every `BasePaginator` subclass (`DateTimePaginator`, `Paginator`, etc.) used across the API.

- For forward cursors, a negative offset is now silently clamped to 0. But `build_cursor` still computes the next cursor from the original negative `cursor.offset`, so the returned next/prev cursors can be wrong (e.g. `offset + limit` stays negative or small).
- For `is_prev` cursors, the negative offset is still passed straight into `queryset[offset:stop]`, which errors.

The comment calling this "safe" is incorrect. Malformed cursors should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` rather than half-handled.

New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests

The PR adds a new paginator, a new query parameter (`optimized_pagination`), and changes the core `BasePaginator.get_result` offset handling, all without tests.

A basic test of `optimized_pagination=true` for an org owner returning audit rows would have exposed the `TypeError` on datetime keys. A test with a negative-offset cursor would have exposed the unsupported negative slice.

Raw numeric cursor value used to filter a datetime column

`value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged. `build_queryset` then emits `WHERE datetime <= %s` with that integer or float.

`DateTimePaginator` instead converts the millisecond value back into a timezone-aware `datetime`. Here the integer is compared against a timestamp column, which either raises a database error or filters incorrectly.

Any cursor-based navigation of audit logs through the optimized path is therefore broken. The paginator should extend `DateTimePaginator` (or reuse its key/value conversion) when ordering by a datetime.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative queryset slicing raises in Django, so the 'advanced' path always errors

When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`. Any request with a cursor such as `0:-10:0` and `optimized_pagination=true` therefore returns a 500 instead of results. The surrounding comments claiming the ORM 'properly handles negative slicing' and that this 'enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' are false. The intent described there is also a security smell. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as `OffsetPaginator` does.

true_positives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comment claims negative offsets are safe for prev cursors in BasePaginator

For `is_prev` cursors the offset is passed through unclamped to queryset slicing. A user-supplied cursor with a negative offset (`Cursor.from_string` accepts one) makes Django raise `ValueError` and the request returns a 500. The comment says 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions', which is incorrect. Negative offsets should be rejected or clamped for both directions.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator key handling breaks on the datetime ordering it is used with

The audit log endpoint uses this paginator with `order_by="-datetime"`. `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on the datetime value, which raises `TypeError` as soon as `build_cursor` computes next/prev cursors on any non-empty page. `value_from_cursor` returns the raw integer cursor value, so `build_queryset` compares the `datetime` column against an integer. The optimized path is unusable even without negative offsets. It needs `DateTimePaginator`'s key/value conversion, or should subclass `DateTimePaginator`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Gate uses raw is_superuser and member may be None

`request.user.is_superuser` is true for superuser accounts even without an active superuser session; Sentry normally checks `is_active_superuser(request)`. `has_global_access` is not an admin-only privilege either: in open-membership orgs every member has it. So this 'admin-only' feature is available far more broadly than intended. In addition, `organization_context.member` can be None (for example staff or token access without membership), in which case `.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError` and the request returns a 500.

false_positives.candidate:
Eviction silently drops earliest-ending spans, including possibly the root span

`zpopmin` removes the spans with the lowest `end_timestamp_precise`. Root/segment spans and other important spans can be discarded without any metric or log. Previously an oversized segment was logged and counted (`segment_span_count_exceeded`). The limit of 1000 is also hardcoded and no longer tied to `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001). That setting is now dead config and the two values disagree.

No test for the new insert-time eviction

The PR's main behavior change is capping segments at 1000 spans by popping the lowest-scored entries in Lua. No test covers it: nothing exercises a segment exceeding the cap, checks which spans survive, or checks interaction with merges via `zunionstore`.

Redirect depth limit reduced 10x and its warning comment removed

The redirect-following loop limit went from 10000 to 1000. Segment trees deeper than 1000 levels will now be split incorrectly. The comment documenting this limitation was deleted, and the PR does not say why the change was made.

Switching span-buf:s keys from SET to ZSET breaks in-flight data during deploy

Keys written by the old code are Redis sets. After deploy, `ZADD`, `ZCARD`, `ZUNIONSTORE` and `ZSCAN` against those keys fail with `WRONGTYPE`. This aborts the whole pipeline or Lua call for the batch and leaves segments unflushable until their TTL (up to an hour) expires. A migration or key-prefix change is needed to roll this out safely.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility checks the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset

`_get_event_stats` passes the closed-over request-level `dataset` to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, not the `scoped_dataset` actually being queried. In the dashboard split path, `scoped_dataset` is `discover` with an `!event.type:transaction` errors query while the outer `dataset` is a metrics dataset. The check then never upsamples the errors split. The opposite mismatch is also possible: the decision is made for one dataset and the transformed columns run against another.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental submodule gitlink committed

The PR adds a `sentry-repo` gitlink (a subproject pointing at the base commit). It has no `.gitmodules` entry and is unrelated to the feature, so it looks like it was committed by mistake. It will confuse checkouts and tooling and should be removed.

Allowlist cache makes changes stale and is never invalidated

Eligibility is cached for 60s in the shared cache. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but nothing calls it, so allowlist changes take up to 60s to apply. The `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` docstring says it 'reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time', which is false once this cache is in front of it. In tests that mock `options`, a value cached by one test can leak into the next test when the same project IDs recur, giving order-dependent results.

Cache round-trip runs before the cheap dataset check and may cost more than it saves

`options.get` is already locally cached, so replacing it with a remote cache get/set (memcached/redis) on every `_get_event_stats` call likely adds latency rather than removing it. The lookup also runs before `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, so requests for spans, transactions or metrics datasets pay for the cache round-trip even though they can never be upsampled.

No tests for the cached entry point or negated queries

The unit tests never exercise `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, so the caching behaviour and cache-key logic are untested. They also do not cover negated or mixed queries such as `!event.type:error` for `_is_error_focused_query`, which is exactly where the substring heuristic fails.

Substring match for event.type:error also matches negated and mixed queries

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the lowercased query contains the substring `event.type:error`. That also matches `!event.type:error`, which excludes errors, and mixed queries such as `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. For the discover dataset this applies `upsampled_count()` (sum of sample_weight) to queries that return transactions or other non-error events. Those rows have no sample_weight, so the reported counts are wrong. The query should be parsed properly instead of substring-matched.

Top-events ordering and selected fields are not transformed

For top events only `timeseries_columns` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()`. `selected_columns` (from `get_field_list`) and `orderby` still use raw `count()`. The top-N groups are therefore chosen by raw count while the plotted values are upsampled, so the two can disagree.

upsampled_count silently undercounts events without sample_weight

`sum(sample_weight)` ignores NULLs, so any event in an allowlisted project that lacks sample_weight counts as 0 instead of 1. Examples are events ingested before the rollout or without client sampling context. The comment assumes the schema guarantees the column is populated, which is not enforced anywhere. Use something like `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))` so missing weights count as one event.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error events zipped against nodestore result dict values by position

`fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids` and calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi`. It then pairs the results with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`, which assumes the returned dict has one entry per requested id, in request order. `get_multi` returns a dict keyed by node_id, and backends do not guarantee that order or that missing keys are present. When they differ, error titles and messages get attached to the wrong event IDs, or entries are silently dropped. Look up each result with `events.get(node_id)` instead of relying on position.

age/timestamp mutual-exclusion check uses truthiness

Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.

false_positives.candidate:
60s deadline for a batch of up to 100 external identity refreshes may break the reschedule chain

`check_auth_identities` refreshes up to `chunk_size=100` identities, and each refresh makes a network call to the SSO provider. It reschedules `check_auth` only at the end of the task. With the new 60s processing deadline, a slow provider can get the task killed before that point. The self-rescheduling chain then stops, and further auth checks depend on the periodic trigger. Raise the deadline or reschedule before processing the batch.

`gen_request_data` interleaves errors with recording events by comparing `error['timestamp']` to `event.get('timestamp')`. The error timestamp comes from nodestore event data and is in seconds since epoch. Top-level rrweb recording-segment event timestamps are in milliseconds. In real data every error therefore sorts before every breadcrumb, so the chronological ordering sent to Seer is wrong. The tests use seconds for both values and do not catch this. Normalize both values to the same unit before comparing.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES only filtered when a search query is present

When `searchQuery` is empty, the memo returns `sorted` before the filter runs. As a result `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` stay visible in the default view and disappear only once the user types a search. Apply the hidden-attribute filter in both branches.

Migrations turned into no-ops that point to a migration not in this PR

Both 0917 and 0920 now just return, with comments directing readers to `0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised.py`. That migration is not added in this change. If it does not already exist, organization saved searches are never converted to GroupSearchViews. Environments that already ran the original 0917 also keep its (allegedly erroneous) results with no corrective migration. The comment that the migration 'was never run' may also be inaccurate, since 0917 shipped with a test and was post-deployment. Add 0921 in this PR or fix the reference.

Per-issue recommended-event lookup when building PR comments

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` once per issue in the comment. Each call issues a Snuba query plus a nodestore fetch, so every comment build adds N sequential round trips. It also swallows all exceptions with only an info log. Consider fetching environments in bulk, or from group tag values.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so one code can be used twice

`authorize` reads `user.backupCodes` at the start of the request, decrypts it, nulls the matched entry and writes the whole blob back. There is no transaction, no optimistic check that the stored ciphertext is unchanged, and no row lock.

Two concurrent sign-ins with the same backup code both see it as valid and both succeed, which breaks the 'usable exactly once' guarantee. Two concurrent sign-ins with different codes can also overwrite each other's update, so one consumed code comes back to life.

Fix: wrap the read and write in a transaction with a conditional update, e.g. `updateMany where { id, backupCodes: <old ciphertext> }` and fail the login if 0 rows are affected.

Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

false_positives.candidate:
2FA is already enabled when the backup-codes step shows, but `onEnable` only runs from the Close button

After a successful `/totp/enable`, the modal now moves to `DisplayBackupCodes` instead of calling `onEnable()`. `onEnable()` and `resetState()` are only invoked by the 'Close' button.

If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape, overlay click, i.e. through `onOpenChange`), the parent never learns that 2FA was enabled. The settings switch keeps showing 2FA as disabled even though it is active server-side. The modal also stays stuck on the backup-codes step for the next open.

Fix: call `onEnable` as soon as the enable succeeds (and only defer closing), or handle dismissal in `onOpenChange` while on that step.

Non-string `backupCode` in the request body causes an unhandled 500

`req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` is called on any truthy value. A JSON body with a numeric or object `backupCode` throws a TypeError and produces a 500 instead of a 400.

The endpoint also throws raw `Error`s instead of returning JSON for the missing-key case, which the client maps to a generic error. Validate the body type before use.

`missing_backup_codes` message points to a regeneration feature that does not exist

Users who enabled 2FA before this migration have `backupCodes = null` and get "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."

There is no UI to generate or regenerate backup codes. The only path is to disable 2FA (which needs a working TOTP code) and enable it again. The message should describe that path, or a regeneration feature should be added.

Fallback lookup for the calendar id can never match

A real `externalId` will never equal a falsy value, so the lookup always returns `undefined`. In `updateEvent`, `calendarId` is then undefined and the update fails. The old behavior of falling back to the destination calendar's externalId (or `"primary"`) is lost.

The new code `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` does the reverse. With billing enabled, the slug is now reserved before payment. Collective hosts' calendars dropped when organizer has no destination calendar

When neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, `evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null`. The later `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` then does nothing. In that case the other collective hosts' destination calendars are silently discarded, which is exactly the multi-host scenario this PR is meant to fix. Hangout-link patch uses an undefined calendarId

The patch request fails, so the Meet link is never added to the event description. Use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` value in both calls.

Recurring cancellation repeats deletes per reference and misses other hosts

The recurring branch now runs inside the per-reference loop, but its body does not depend on the reference. It iterates all of the organizer's credentials and deletes the first calendar reference of every updated booking. With N references, the same deletes run N times. Because it only uses `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` and `.find` (one reference per booking), the other collective hosts' recurring events are never deleted.

`updateAllCalendarEvents` now handles multiple calendar references, one per host. Updates that look up video credentials by reference will break too.

The rewritten `loadUsers` no longer selects `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` for dynamic users. Code that relies on the user's organization slug, such as building org booker URLs, will get undefined for dynamic group bookings. This refactor is unrelated to the destination-calendar fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Placeholder refresh_token overwrites the real stored refresh token

When the provider response has no `refresh_token`, the function sets it to the literal string "refresh_token". Office365 then spreads this over the stored credential (`{...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data}`), which replaces the real refresh token with "refresh_token".

Microsoft does not always return a new refresh token. This happens even when sync is disabled, so later refreshes fail and the credential is permanently broken.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys do not do what the comments claim

`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal key "[object Object]". Because the keys are duplicates, the second one wins, so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]"?: unknown }`.

Zod strips unknown keys by default. In sync mode every other field is dropped: `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, `scope`, `token_type` and so on.

Consequences:
- Zoom computes `Date.now() + undefined*1000` = NaN for the expiry.
- Office365 loses its expiry.
- Nothing actually validates that an expiry is present.

Use `.passthrough()` or `z.record`/`catchall` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google credential key is overwritten with the safeParse result wrapper

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns a zod `SafeParseReturnType` (`{ success, data }`), not the parsed token. Before this change the code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(...)`, which is the token itself. Now `key` is the wrapper object and is written to the DB as `{ key }`.

After the first refresh, every Google Calendar credential is stored as `{success:true,data:{...}}`. The next `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` in the constructor then fails, breaking the integration for all users, including those who never enabled sync.

Store `key.data` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

false_positives.candidate:
Outbound credential-sync request carries no authentication

The POST to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug`. There is no secret, signature or auth header.

The self-hoster's endpoint returns live access tokens, but it has no way to verify the caller is Cal.com. Anyone who can reach that endpoint can obtain any user's third-party tokens by enumerating user IDs.

Wrong app slug sent for Zoom

The slug "zoomvideo" is passed to `refreshOAuthTokens`, but Zoom's app slug/appId is "zoom". The callback uses `appId: "zoom"`, and the webhook stores credentials by `appMetadata.slug`. The sync endpoint will receive a slug that does not match the one used everywhere else.

prisma used without import in Salesforce CalendarService

Duplicate and blacklist checks are case-sensitive

The blacklist entries are lowercased, but the incoming guest emails are not. An address like `Foo@x.com` therefore bypasses a blacklisted `foo@x.com`. Team admin/owner check uses && so only users who pass both checks qualify

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. The variable name says either role should be enough, but the `&&` means a team admin who is not an owner fails the check. Such admins are rejected with FORBIDDEN unless they are the organizer or an attendee. Use `||`, or a single admin-or-owner query.

Existing attendees whose emails were resubmitted are treated as new and get a fresh 'scheduled' email instead of the 'guests added' notification. Pass `uniqueGuests`.

sendAddGuestsEmails ignores disabled standard emails and seated-event attendee privacy

Unlike the other senders in this file, `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no `eventTypeMetadata` and never checks `disableStandardEmails`. Hosts and attendees therefore get emails even when the event type disables them. It also sends every attendee the full calEvent, attendee list included, without honoring `seatsShowAttendees`. Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can add unlimited arbitrary guests and trigger emails sent in the organizer's name

Authorization lets any booking attendee call this mutation. Nothing checks booking status (cancelled, past, rejected), and the input schema has no max length on `guests`. So any attendee can insert arbitrary attendee rows and make the system send emails to any addresses, with the organizer's name and reply-to. This is a spam/abuse vector. It also ignores seat limits on seated events. Restrict who can add guests, cap the list size, and validate booking state.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

The EventManager is built from `ctx.user`'s credentials. When the caller is an attendee or a team admin rather than the organizer, `updateCalendarAttendees` runs with credentials that do not own the booking's calendar references. The external calendar event then is not updated, or the call throws. The booking user's credentials are already loaded (`booking.user.credentials`) and should be used instead.

DB write happens before an unguarded calendar update; a failure leaves inconsistent state

Attendees are written to the DB first. `updateCalendarAttendees` is then awaited without try/catch. If it throws, the client gets an error even though the guests were persisted. No emails are sent, and a retry fails with `emails_must_be_unique_valid` because the guests now exist. Wrap the external update and emails so a failure there cannot leave this half-done state, or roll back.

Error toast fallback is unreachable and can show 'undefined:'

`message` is a template string, so it is always a non-empty string and the `|| t("unable_to_add_guests")` fallback never runs. When `err.data?.code` is undefined, for example on a network error, the toast reads 'undefined: ...'.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

Non-atomic retryCount increment

The new count is computed as `reminder.retryCount + 1` from the value read at fetch time. If two cron invocations overlap, increments can be lost. Use Prisma's atomic `{ increment: 1 }` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount deletion branch is not scoped to SMS reminders

The new `OR` branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter. This SMS cron will therefore delete any WorkflowReminder (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) whose retryCount exceeds 1. Today only this handler increments the field, but retryCount is a shared column on WorkflowReminder. Once the email or WhatsApp schedulers start using it with their own retry policy, this job will silently delete their reminders. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` to that branch.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders with no sendTo or empty message are never counted as failures

retryCount is only incremented when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy or throws. If `sendTo` is missing (e.g. no smsReminderNumber) or the generated message is empty, the reminder is skipped without incrementing. The same happens for reminders skipped by the `!reminder.workflowStep || !reminder.booking` check. These reminders keep being re-fetched every cron run until their scheduled date, which is the exact behaviour this PR is meant to stop.

Unguarded DB update inside catch can abort the whole cron run

The `prisma.workflowReminder.update` in the `catch` block is not wrapped in its own try/catch. It can throw, for example if the record was deleted concurrently because the booking was cancelled or rescheduled, or on a transient DB error. If it does, the exception escapes the for-loop and the handler. All remaining reminders in that batch go unprocessed and the cron returns an error. The same applies to the retry-increment update in the `else` branch. Wrap the increment so a failure there only logs.

Deferred cancellation misses reminders scheduled shortly after the booking is cancelled

Cancelling a booking now only sets `cancelled: true`. The real SendGrid cancel happens in the cron, which runs every 15 minutes.

If the booking is cancelled when its reminder is less than about 15 minutes from `sendAt`, the next cron run may come too late. SendGrid needs the cancel some minutes before send time, or the run may come after the send. The email is then delivered for a cancelled booking. Before this change the cancel was sent immediately.

Fix: cancel immediately when `scheduledDate` is already inside the cron's one-hour window, and defer only reminders scheduled further out.

All cancellations run sequentially inside a single try. If any `client.request` throws, the loop stops and `Promise.all(workflowRemindersToDelete)` is never reached. Prisma queries are lazy, so none of the queued deletes run, including those for batches SendGrid already cancelled successfully.

On the next cron run the same reminders are returned again. SendGrid rejects a second cancel for a batch that already has a status, so the same first reminder throws on every run. Every cancelled reminder after it in the list then never gets cancelled, and those emails go out until the stale row ages past `scheduledDate`.

Fix: wrap each reminder in its own try/catch, delete the row right after a successful cancel, and treat an 'already cancelled' response as success.

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` (`slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`), so it is identical to `start`. The `end > workingHour.endTime` comparison never detects a slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end. It should use `slotEndTime`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === (always false)

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two distinct object references, so it is always false. The intended 'override with zero length = unavailable all day' branch never runs. For such an override, a slot starting exactly at the override instant passes the remaining before/after checks and is treated as available. Use `.isSame()` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
No test for the round-robin fixed-host date override fix

The PR's main fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides restrict round-robin availability, and it adds new override and working-hours logic to `checkIfIsAvailable`. Only a single-user timezone case is tested. Nothing covers:
- A round-robin event with fixed and loose hosts.
- Users with working hours crossing UTC midnight or split ranges.
- Slots overlapping override boundaries.

These are exactly the scenarios where the bugs above occur.

Override date matching mixes server-local and UTC calendar days

Two problems in matching an override to a slot's day:
- The override day is computed with `dayjs(date.start)...format("YYYY MM DD")`, which uses the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime` is UTC. On non-UTC servers the dates can mismatch.
- Matching is by UTC calendar day, not by the organizer's local day the override applies to. For organizers far from UTC (e.g. PST), regular-hours slots from the previous local day that share the UTC date get evaluated against the override and wrongly rejected. Conversely, override hours on the other UTC date are not matched.

Parsing Date.toString() output with dayjs is non-standard

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` relies on `new Date()` parsing the locale-style string from `Date.toString()` (e.g. "Tue Mar 21 2023 ... GMT+0000 (Coordinated Universal Time)"). This format is implementation-defined and drops milliseconds. Passing the Date directly, `dayjs(override.start)`, is reliable.

Shifted override minutes wrap around midnight and get dropped

After adding the invitee/organizer offset, start and end are converted to minute-of-day via `hour()*60+minute()`. If the shift moves an override across the invitee's midnight (e.g. 22:00–02:00 in invitee time), endTime becomes smaller than startTime and `buildSlots` discards the range. `activeOverrides` is also still filtered on the unshifted `dayjs.utc(override.start)` date, so for large offsets the override can land on the wrong invitee day. Slots on the adjacent day are then missing or incorrect.

Slots overlapping the end of a date override are accepted

The only end-side rejection is `slotStartTime.isAfter(overrideEnd)`. Two cases slip through:
- A slot starting exactly at the override end.
- A slot that starts inside the override but ends after it, e.g. a 60-min slot starting 30 minutes before the end.

Both are considered available, so fixed hosts can still be booked outside their override window. The check should reject when `slotEndTime` is after the override end, or when `slotStartTime` is the same as or after it.

Working-hours check rejects slots that fall outside any one of several working-hour ranges

The `workingHours.find(...)` returns true, meaning unavailable, as soon as any single working-hour entry for that weekday does not contain the slot.

Users with more than one range on the same day therefore lose slots. Examples:
- A split day such as 9–12 and 13–17.
- A schedule crossing UTC midnight, which `getWorkingHours` splits into two entries (e.g. 1020–1439 on day N and 0–60 on day N+1).

A slot inside one range is always outside the other, so it is rejected. The check must instead verify that the slot lies within at least one matching range. Otherwise US-timezone organizers, and anyone with split hours, can lose most or all slots.

Test sleep is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

The test patches `time.sleep` to `lambda _: None` at the start. The later `time.sleep(0.1)`, meant to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change", therefore does nothing. CLI default contradicts the factory/flusher default of one process per shard

join() never terminates spawned processes
