true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting implementation; passes only by timing

In `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, the worker completes offsets in `finally` even on exceptions. Offsets 100 and 101 therefore become committable and are committed on the next 1s tick of the commit loop.

The test asserts that no commit happened, and it only passes because it checks before the commit loop fires. That makes it flaky. It also contradicts its own docstring, which says errors should not block commits.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function` there, which invokes the Arroyo `Commit` callable. That callable stages offsets on the `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`, which are single-threaded and not thread-safe. This races with `poll`/`stage_offsets` on the main thread.

It can also commit offsets for partitions that were already revoked, because the commit thread and workers keep running during a rebalance. Offsets should be collected in the background but committed from the strategy's `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread.

Commits stall permanently on natural Kafka offset gaps

`get_committable_offsets` stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transactional control markers and compacted topics both leave gaps. Any such gap means the committed offset never advances past it, even though every received message is processed.

The result is ever-growing reported lag and full reprocessing on restart. The contiguity check should only consider offsets that were actually received, for example by advancing to the minimum outstanding offset minus 1, or to the max seen when nothing is outstanding.

Failed processing still marks offset complete; docstring claims commit only after success

The `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raised, so failed messages are committed. That contradicts the class guarantee "Only commits offsets after successful processing".

Either the behavior or the documentation should change.

Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently shut down on first rebalance, silently dropping messages afterwards

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory `__init__`. Every strategy from `create_with_partitions` reuses it, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and stops the workers.

Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation, so after the first rebalance the next strategy gets a dead pool. `work_queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit` catches it and marks the offset as completed. As a result every subsequent message is skipped without being processed, yet its offset is committed. This is silent data loss.

The pool should be owned by the strategy (created per `create_with_partitions`), or the strategy should not shut down a factory-owned pool.

Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim

Each `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow group therefore lets its queue grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling Kafka, so memory grows unbounded.

The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is false. Bound the queues and reject or pause when they are full.

close() stops committing before workers drain, so processed work is never committed

`close()` first sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread. Only after that does it shut down the pool, which lets workers finish their remaining queued items. There is no final commit.

Items completed during that drain, plus anything completed in the last second before shutdown, are never committed. They get reprocessed after every rebalance or restart. Drain the workers first, then perform one final commit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not prove the denial cache short-circuits

The comment says the permCache entry grants access, but it sets {"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats that as not allowed. The DB fallback also returns no permissions, because the default fakeStore has none. The test would therefore pass with the denial cache removed entirely. The cache entry should be true, and the store should grant access, so the test actually verifies the short-circuit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key is ambiguous because '_' can appear inside names and folder UIDs

userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_', and resource names and folder UIDs may contain underscores. For example, (name="a_b", parent="") and (name="a", parent="b_") both produce "..._a_b_". A denial recorded for one resource/folder pair is then returned for a different one, giving a false deny for up to 30s. Use a separator that cannot occur in these values, or encode the components.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
DB fallback still uses the cached folder tree, so access via a newly created parent folder is denied and the denial cached

On a cache miss or stale-cache deny, Check re-fetches permissions from the DB. checkPermission then calls checkInheritedPermissions, which uses buildFolderTree, served from folderCache (30s TTL). A folder created after the tree was cached has no ancestors in that tree. If the user's grant is on an ancestor of the new folder, the check fails even with fresh permissions, and the result is written to the denial cache. Newly created folder hierarchies therefore still yield false denials for up to 30s, which is the scenario this PR is meant to fix.

Denials are cached for 30s and checked before any requery, reintroducing the stale-access problem

A denied Check stores a denial entry for shortCacheTTL (30s). That entry is read at the top of Check, before the cached permissions and before the DB fallback. If a check runs in the window before a newly created dashboard/folder's permission rows are visible, the denial is cached. The same happens when an admin grants access to a resource the user was just denied. In both cases every later Check for that resource returns denied for up to 30s without consulting the DB. The DB requery, which this PR adds specifically to fix creator access, is skipped. Nothing invalidates denial entries when permissions change.

Every deny on cached permissions now triggers a full DB permission query

Previously a warm permCache answered Check entirely from cache. Now any check that is denied from cached permissions falls through to getIdentityPermissions. That path issues team, basic-role and permission queries; getUserPermissions no longer consults the cache. Singleflight only collapses concurrent identical requests, and the denial cache is per resource. A user checked against many resources they cannot access, such as filtering a dashboard list with per-item Check, now causes one DB round trip per denied resource every 30s. This can substantially increase DB load.

List still serves stale cached permissions, so newly created resources are missing from listings

List returns the cached permission map whenever one exists and never requeries. A dashboard or folder the user just created (and only has a direct grant on) will not appear in List results for up to 30s. This is inconsistent with Check, which now falls back to the DB, and leaves part of the described problem unfixed.

Clicking it sets `showSilenceDrawer`, but the drawer only renders when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. `rule` is now undefined in the list view, so clicking the item silently does nothing.

false_positives.candidate:

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range detection runs on interpolated expr, so range-variable queries are now split

`runSplitQuery` now calls `applyTemplateVariables` on every query before partitioning. `querySupportsSplitting()` then calls `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` on the result. That function looks for the literal `$__range` text, which `templateSrv.replace` has already substituted, so the check no longer matches. Queries using `$__range`/`$__range_s`/`$__range_ms` will be split into daily chunks. As the code comment explains, those queries must not be split. Each chunk then evaluates a range-sized window and the merged result is wrong (e.g. `count_over_time(...[$__range])` summed over chunks). Run the splitting check on the raw target expression before interpolation, or keep the original expr around for it.

Empty-expr filter now runs before interpolation

Previously `interpolateVariablesInQueries` ran first and the `query.expr` filter ran on the interpolated result. Now the filter runs on the raw expr and interpolation happens afterwards. A query whose expr is just a variable that resolves to an empty string is no longer dropped and gets sent for execution and sharding. The same ordering applies in `runSplitQuery`. Filter on the interpolated expr instead.

Queries are interpolated and ad-hoc filters applied multiple times

The splitter now calls `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`. The sub-requests then go through `datasource.runQuery` (DataSourceWithBackend.query), which calls `applyTemplateVariables` again on each target with the same `filters`. In the sharding path it happens three times: `runShardSplitQuery`, then `runSplitQuery`, then the backend query. The test now asserts 5 calls.

Re-applying ad-hoc filters can add duplicate label matchers or filter stages. Re-interpolating an already interpolated expression can expand `$`-sequences that came from variable values, and can double-escape regex-escaped values. Interpolate once, or strip `filters`/scopedVars from the sub-request so later stages don't re-apply them.

Returning `f` (or a logger that shares the same `Logs` storage) would keep the recordings.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface breaks other implementations

`FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` is now a required method on the exported `plog.Logger` interface. Any other implementation of `plog.Logger` stops compiling until it adds this method. That includes fakes and wrappers in other packages and in enterprise or external code. The change goes beyond the rename the PR title describes.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware and the changed LoggerMiddleware fields have no tests

The plugin/request log fields (pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, uname) used to be added explicitly in `LoggerMiddleware`. They now depend on `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` setting contextual attributes, and on that middleware sitting before `LoggerMiddleware` in the chain. No test checks that `instrumentContext` sets these attributes or that the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line still carries them and the traceID. true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert is not atomic; limit can be exceeded under concurrency

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` runs `CountDevices` and then does a separate INSERT, with no transaction or lock. Concurrent first requests from new devices, or several Grafana instances sharing one DB, can all read `count < limit` and all insert. The configured limit can then be exceeded by an arbitrary amount.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rowsAffected==0 treated as limit reached; false positives on MySQL

`updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `RowsAffected()` is 0. By default MySQL reports only rows whose values actually changed, not rows matched. `updated_at` has second precision, so an existing, already-counted device re-tagged within the same second with the same IP and user agent changes nothing and gets 0 rows. That device is then wrongly rejected as over the limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit only enforced on first request; cache entry lets rejected devices in afterwards

`tagDeviceUI` writes the device key to the local cache before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, and it does not remove the key when that call fails. When the limit is hit, the first request returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and `Authenticate` rejects it. Every later request from the same device in the next ~29 minutes hits the cache and returns nil, so `Authenticate` succeeds. The limit therefore only rejects a device's first request and is not actually enforced. Fix by evicting the key on error, or by setting the cache only after a successful store call.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit bypassed by omitting the device ID header

`TagDevice` returns nil when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is missing, and it also returns nil when the IP cannot be parsed. In both cases anonymous authentication succeeds without any limit check. Any client can get unlimited anonymous access by not sending the header, so the limit is advisory at best.

Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path

Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own timeout and panic recovery. It now runs inline in `Authenticate`, using the request context. When a limit is configured, each new device costs an extra COUNT(*) query plus a write. Slow-DB latency, or a panic in this path, now directly affects every anonymous request. The previous panic protection was also removed.

No test that existing devices can still be updated at the limit

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only checks that a new device is rejected once the limit is reached. No test checks that an already-registered device is still updated successfully at the limit, which is the `updateDevice` path. No test covers the authn client behaviour either, including repeat requests after a rejection.

Provider signature changes likely break wire DI

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now takes `db.DB` instead of `anonstore.AnonStore`. `ProvideAnonDBStore` now takes an extra `int64` that wire cannot supply. No wire set (wire.go / wireexts) is updated in this PR. If `ProvideAnonDBStore` is still registered as a provider there, wire generation fails. Otherwise the unused binding should be removed.

anonymousDeviceLimit inferred as type `undefined`

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` has no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the class property type as `undefined`, not `number | undefined`. Consumers of `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` cannot use it as a number without casting. Declare it as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left at Error level, dumping full ID lists every batch

Each cleanup batch logs at Error level with the full slice of fetched IDs, the SQL condition and a nil error. This happens at lines 534/537 (by time), 554/557 (by count) and 576/579 (orphaned tags). With batch sizes up to tens of thousands, every batch writes huge log lines. Healthy runs will flood the logs and trigger error-based alerting. The final no-op batch also logs at Error level. These look like leftover debugging statements and should be removed or lowered to Debug without the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

The ticker for all cleanup jobs went from 10 minutes to 1 minute, while each run still has a 9-minute timeout. This affects snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history and annotations. It is unrelated to the deadlock fix, is not mentioned in the PR description, and looks like a leftover local testing change. It multiplies DB load by 10x and makes contention with the annotation write path more likely, which works against the stated goal of reducing deadlocks. Revert it.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder path can exceed MySQL/Postgres bind-parameter limits for large batch sizes

On non-SQLite databases, each ID becomes a bound parameter. MySQL and Postgres cap prepared statements at 65535 parameters. If `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` is configured above that, the DELETE fails on every run and cleanup never progresses. The old subquery-based statement had no such limit. Either chunk the IDs or inline them for all dialects.

Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite

The SQLite inline path builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop. Each iteration copies the whole accumulated string, so the cost is O(n^2). This path only runs when the batch size exceeds 999, i.e. for large batches such as the 32767 used in the test, so tens of thousands of IDs mean hundreds of MB of copying per batch. Use a strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the base logger in context instead of the enriched one

`ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the base logger rather than `log`. Downstream storage logs therefore lack the name, kind and method values, unlike the other methods.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection recorded as a storage duration

The background legacy DeleteCollection calls `d.recordStorageDuration` rather than `recordLegacyDuration`. Each delete-collection is counted twice as a storage operation and never as a legacy one, which skews both metric series.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object name used as the metric 'kind' label in Delete

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object name where the kind belongs. Every object name becomes a separate label value, causing unbounded Prometheus cardinality and wrong kind attribution. It should be `options.Kind`.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get canceled when the request returns

Each background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the incoming request context. The method returns as soon as the unified-storage write succeeds, and the apiserver then cancels the request context. That cancellation reaches the derived context, so the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is often aborted or never runs (same pattern at lines 110, 135, 163). Legacy storage silently drifts from unified storage, which defeats the stated 'safe measure'. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the timeout.

Legacy update re-applies objInfo against legacy state instead of the unified result

The previous code wrapped the unified-storage result in `updateWrapper`, so legacy received exactly the object written to unified storage. Now the raw `objInfo` is replayed in a goroutine, and the update or patch is applied to whatever old object legacy holds. For PATCH/apply, or when the stores already differ, legacy ends up with different content than unified storage. Reusing `objInfo` concurrently after the request has finished is also unsafe.

Legacy write failures in background goroutines are never logged

The goroutines only record a duration metric with an error flag. The error itself is discarded in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection. The old code logged legacy failures. Now a divergence between legacy and unified storage leaves no trace of which object failed or why.

Mode 3 integration tests check legacy reads immediately after async writes

`doPlaylistTests` creates or updates through k8s and then immediately queries the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints via `getFromBothAPIs` and the search check. In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these assertions race the background goroutine. If the legacy endpoint reads legacy storage, the test will be flaky; if it reads unified storage, legacy consistency is not being tested at all.

Request object shared with a background goroutine while the handler keeps using it

`obj` and `options` are passed to `d.Legacy.Create` in a goroutine after the method has already returned `created`, which may be the same pointer or derived from `obj`. The apiserver goes on encoding or mutating the response while legacy storage reads or mutates the same object, which is a data race. The object should be deep-copied before handing it to the goroutine.

Storage create failure recorded as a legacy duration

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Unified-storage failures are therefore reported as legacy failures. The same mistake is in Update at line 129.

Unit tests never verify the async legacy write and race with it

The tests return right after the dual-writer call without waiting for the background goroutine, so nothing asserts that the legacy write happens. Legacy and storage mocks share a single `mock.Mock`, so expectations meant for one store satisfy calls to the other. For example, the 'unified store fails' Create case only fails because the legacy expectation for `failingObj` is matched by the storage call. A goroutine can also invoke the mock after the subtest finishes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of the cache after taking the write lock

`GetWebAssets` reads the cache under `RLock`, releases it, then takes the exclusive `Lock`. It never re-checks `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring that lock.

When the cache is empty (startup, or after a failed load), every concurrent caller that saw `nil` queues on the write lock. Each one then re-reads and re-parses `assets-manifest.json` in turn, even though the first one already filled the cache.

This redundant reload can also lose a good value. If a later goroutine's reload fails (e.g. a transient read error), it sets `entryPointAssetsCache = result` with `nil`. That overwrites the valid cache the first goroutine just stored, and the caller gets an error that a simple re-check would have avoided.

Fix: after `Lock()`, add `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`. Alternatively, only assign the cache when `err == nil`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false; the feature flag is silently dead

`enableSqlExpressions` negates the `sqlExpressions` flag, then returns false in both branches. The flag lookup has no effect, and the function name suggests the flag still controls the feature. Replace this with a plain `return false` (or remove the check) plus a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264. Also mark the flag as deprecated or no-op in the registry and docs.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing SQL parser/command tests will break against the stub DB

`TablesList` now goes through the stub `DB.RunCommands`, which always returns "not implemented". `TablesList` therefore always fails, and `NewSQLCommand` always returns the `sql-invalid-sql` BadRequest. The existing tests that assert parsed table names and successful SQL command creation (in `pkg/expr/sql` parser tests and `pkg/expr` SQL command tests) were not updated or skipped in this PR, so CI will fail. Those tests should be skipped or rewritten to assert the new disabled behaviour.

false_positives.candidate:
Dead DuckDB code path left in place, including SQL string building and logging of raw user SQL

`TablesList` still builds a hand-escaped `json_serialize_sql('%s')` command, which was the injection vector. On every call it now logs the full user SQL and the command at Error level, because the stub always fails. The variable is still named `duckDB`. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same key

With the coarse lock gone, nothing stops two callers from building the same NamespacedResource at once. Callers include `getOrCreateIndex` from Search (including federated lookups) and from `handleEvent`, and the init workers. Each caller sees `GetIndex == nil` and calls `BuildIndex`.

For in-memory indexes, one fully built index silently replaces the other. Writes applied to the losing index by a concurrent watch event are lost, and the IndexTenants/IndexedKinds metrics are double counted.

For file-based indexes (`size > FileThreshold`), both callers run `bleve.New` on the same directory and the second fails. A per-key singleflight or lock is needed to keep the speedup without this race.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates cache map without lock while builds can now write it concurrently

`BuildIndex` no longer holds `cacheMu` for its whole body; it now writes `b.cache[key]` under a short lock. `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu` at all.

In `searchSupport.init`, the watch goroutine is started (search.go:207) before `s.search.TotalDocs()` is called (search.go:216). `handleEvent` -> `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex` can therefore write the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating it. Search requests can do the same once the server is up.

Concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error in Go and will crash the process. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Context cancel leaked when Init fails in constructor

`NewResourceServer` creates `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` and then returns `nil, err` if `s.Init(ctx)` fails, without calling `cancel`.

Any goroutines or watchers started during partial initialization keep running. For example, the search watch goroutine may already be started if only `initWatcher` failed. They are never cancelled.

`cancel()` should be called on the error path.

Init worker goroutines race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`

Inside `group.Go`, each goroutine assigns the outer `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` with no synchronization. Both are data races.

This PR's goal is to make these builds actually run in parallel by removing the backend lock, which makes the races far more likely to bite. One goroutine's error can be overwritten by another, and the reported count is unreliable.

The goroutine should use a local `err` and an atomic counter.

Postgres integration test skipped instead of fixed

The storage-server module test is now skipped for postgres in CI. This likely follows from the behaviour change to eager initialization in the constructor, which is exactly what the test exercises.

Skipping it removes coverage for eager init against postgres, the scenario the PR description itself asks reviewers to worry about. It should be fixed, or the root cause should be documented.

Requests are no longer rejected after Stop

`Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". Previously every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returned that `initErr`, so requests were rejected after shutdown.

This PR removes those `Init` calls from all handlers. After `Stop`, Create/Read/List/Watch/etc. now run against a stopped backend instead of returning a clean error. `initErr` is effectively dead after construction.

Either keep a cheap stopped/initErr check in the handlers or remove the now-meaningless assignments.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public SPI interface `CryptoProvider`. Any third-party or out-of-tree implementation (custom crypto providers, older keycloak-client copies) will fail to compile. Already-compiled implementations will hit `AbstractMethodError` when `detectProvider` calls `order()`. A `default` method returning a neutral value would preserve compatibility.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers now resolve silently and nondeterministically

`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return order 200. If two of them are on the classpath (e.g. FIPS plus default), selection depends on ServiceLoader iteration, which is effectively classpath order. Previously this case threw an `IllegalStateException`. Now it only logs at debug level. As a result, a deployment intended to run in FIPS mode could silently pick the non-FIPS provider. Keep failing when more than one provider shares the highest order, or give the providers distinct orders.

Ignored providers are still instantiated and mutate global JCA state

`detectProvider` now iterates the whole `ServiceLoader` and sorts the results. That instantiates every `CryptoProvider` on the classpath, including the ones that end up ignored. These constructors have global side effects:
- `FIPS1402Provider` calls `Security.insertProviderAt` to put KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider, BCFIPS and BCJSSE at positions 1-3, and changes the ssl.KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory security properties.
- `DefaultCryptoProvider` registers BouncyCastle.

Before this change, having several providers on the classpath was a hard error, so the side effects could not go unnoticed. Now a provider that is 'ignored' (only reported in a debug log) can still reorder JVM security providers and TLS defaults. Ordering should be resolved without instantiating every provider, for example via `ServiceLoader.stream()` or a static order, or the side effects should be moved out of the constructors.

Test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and never verifies the re-encoded DER

The key pair is generated with the default EC size (P-256) and reused for ES384 and ES512. As a result, r and s are always about 32 bytes, and the 48- and 66-byte cases (including P-521 values with leading bytes) are never exercised. The test also only checks that DER -> RS -> DER -> RS round-trips to the same RS. It never checks that the produced DER is accepted by `Signature.verify`, or that it matches the existing BC implementation, so a symmetric encoding bug would pass. Use curve-appropriate keys (secp384r1, secp521r1) and verify the reconstructed DER signature.

canManage() is granted by VIEW permission on all groups

`canManage()` falls back to `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`. An admin who only holds the VIEW scope on the all-groups resource therefore passes `canManage()`. That check guards top-level group creation and moving groups (`GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup` → `requireManage()`), and it is also reached through `canView(group)`-style checks in the parent class. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses resource ids and the wrong type lookup

In V2, per-group resources are created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource`. Their name is the group id and no type is set, so `findByType(server, "Groups")` only returns the all-groups resource named "Groups".

The callback then does `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)`, which looks the resource up by name using its id. That lookup always misses and falls back to the all-groups resource. It then adds `groupResource.getId()`, a resource id rather than a group id, to the result.

canManage() javadoc documents VIEW as granting manage

Admin UI message switched to Java MessageFormat, which i18next won't interpolate

- a locale name that the `_[a-zA-Z-_]*` regex does not rewrite as expected.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hung flusher processes are never killed before a replacement is spawned

In production the flusher creates processes with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which yields `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.Process`, so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is False and `process.kill()` is never called.

The old code called `kill()` unconditionally. Now, when a process is detected as hung (`cause = "hang"`), a new process is started for the same shards while the old one keeps running. Two flushers then work the same Redis shards concurrently, which can produce duplicate or fragmented segments and leaks a process on every restart.

Fix: check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, or test for `threading.Thread` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently shut down on first rebalance, silently dropping messages afterwards

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory `__init__`. Every strategy from `create_with_partitions` reuses it, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and stops the workers.

Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation, so after the first rebalance the next strategy gets a dead pool. `work_queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit` catches it and marks the offset as completed. As a result every subsequent message is skipped without being processed, yet its offset is committed. This is silent data loss.

The pool should be owned by the strategy (created per `create_with_partitions`), or the strategy should not shut down a factory-owned pool.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function` there, which invokes the Arroyo `Commit` callable. That callable stages offsets on the `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`, which are single-threaded and not thread-safe. This races with `poll`/`stage_offsets` on the main thread.

It can also commit offsets for partitions that were already revoked, because the commit thread and workers keep running during a rebalance. Offsets should be collected in the background but committed from the strategy's `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread.

Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim

Each `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow group therefore lets its queue grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling Kafka, so memory grows unbounded.

The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is false. Bound the queues and reject or pause when they are full.

Commits stall permanently on natural Kafka offset gaps

`get_committable_offsets` stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transactional control markers and compacted topics both leave gaps. Any such gap means the committed offset never advances past it, even though every received message is processed.

The result is ever-growing reported lag and full reprocessing on restart. The contiguity check should only consider offsets that were actually received, for example by advancing to the minimum outstanding offset minus 1, or to the max seen when nothing is outstanding.

close() stops committing before workers drain, so processed work is never committed

`close()` first sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread. Only after that does it shut down the pool, which lets workers finish their remaining queued items. There is no final commit.

Items completed during that drain, plus anything completed in the last second before shutdown, are never committed. They get reprocessed after every rebalance or restart. Drain the workers first, then perform one final commit.

Failed processing still marks offset complete; docstring claims commit only after success

The `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raised, so failed messages are committed. That contradicts the class guarantee "Only commits offsets after successful processing".

Either the behavior or the documentation should change.

Quadratic string building when inlining IDs for SQLite

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and get canceled when the request returns

Each background goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` from the incoming request context. The method returns as soon as the unified-storage write succeeds, and the apiserver then cancels the request context. That cancellation reaches the derived context, so the legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection is often aborted or never runs (same pattern at lines 110, 135, 163). Legacy storage silently drifts from unified storage, which defeats the stated 'safe measure'. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` before applying the timeout.

Legacy write failures in background goroutines are never logged

The goroutines only record a duration metric with an error flag. The error itself is discarded in Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection. The old code logged legacy failures. Now a divergence between legacy and unified storage leaves no trace of which object failed or why.

Storage create failure recorded as a legacy duration

When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`. Unified-storage failures are therefore reported as legacy failures. The same mistake is in Update at line 129.

Legacy update re-applies objInfo against legacy state instead of the unified result

The previous code wrapped the unified-storage result in `updateWrapper`, so legacy received exactly the object written to unified storage. Now the raw `objInfo` is replayed in a goroutine, and the update or patch is applied to whatever old object legacy holds. For PATCH/apply, or when the stores already differ, legacy ends up with different content than unified storage. Reusing `objInfo` concurrently after the request has finished is also unsafe.

Request object shared with a background goroutine while the handler keeps using it

`obj` and `options` are passed to `d.Legacy.Create` in a goroutine after the method has already returned `created`, which may be the same pointer or derived from `obj`. The apiserver goes on encoding or mutating the response while legacy storage reads or mutates the same object, which is a data race. The object should be deep-copied before handing it to the goroutine.

Unit tests never verify the async legacy write and race with it

The tests return right after the dual-writer call without waiting for the background goroutine, so nothing asserts that the legacy write happens. Legacy and storage mocks share a single `mock.Mock`, so expectations meant for one store satisfy calls to the other. For example, the 'unified store fails' Create case only fails because the legacy expectation for `failingObj` is matched by the storage call. A goroutine can also invoke the mock after the subtest finishes.

Mode 3 integration tests check legacy reads immediately after async writes

`doPlaylistTests` creates or updates through k8s and then immediately queries the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints via `getFromBothAPIs` and the search check. In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these assertions race the background goroutine. If the legacy endpoint reads legacy storage, the test will be flaky; if it reads unified storage, legacy consistency is not being tested at all.

$__range detection runs on interpolated expr, so range-variable queries are now split

Queries are interpolated and ad-hoc filters applied multiple times

Re-interpolating an already interpolated expression can expand `$`-sequences that came from variable values, and can double-escape regex-escaped values. A query whose expr is just a variable that resolves to an empty string is no longer dropped and gets sent for execution and sharding. The same ordering applies in `runSplitQuery`. false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded in the web request path, not in jobs or mailers

With the accelerator patch, translations load on demand. `I18n.translate` only loads `config.locale`, and the fallback locales (site default and `:en`) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`. That call happens solely in `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks and other non-controller code never call it. In those contexts the Fallbacks backend looks up keys in locales that were never loaded and gets nil, so fallbacks silently do not work and users see 'translation missing' text. The fallback locales should be loaded inside `I18n.translate`/`load_locale`, not in a controller filter.

Translation cache key ignores the fallback chain, so stale or missing results stay cached

Results now depend on the fallback chain: `SiteSetting.default_locale`, plus which fallback locales happen to be loaded. The LRU cache key is still only key + `config.locale` + backend id. Two problems follow. (1) If the site's default locale changes, cached fallback strings from the old default locale keep being served until the process restarts or the entry is evicted. (2) If a key is translated before the fallback locales are loaded (e.g. outside a controller), the 'translation missing' result is frozen into the cache. It is then returned even after the fallback locales are loaded. The cache key should include the fallback chain, or the cache should be cleared when the default locale changes.

SiteSetting lookup on every fallback resolution

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds a new array and reads `SiteSetting.default_locale` on every call. The Fallbacks backend calls it on every uncached translate, which includes every translate call that has interpolation or count arguments, since those bypass the LRU cache. This allocates a new array on every one of those calls and adds avoidable overhead to a very hot path.

No tests for new fallback behavior

The PR changes translation resolution for every locale but adds no specs. Untested cases include: fallback to the site locale then to English, loading of the fallback locales, and behavior in non-request contexts. Regressions such as the missing-load issue in jobs would go unnoticed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

Working-hours check rejects slots that fall outside any one of several working-hour ranges

The `workingHours.find(...)` returns true, meaning unavailable, as soon as any single working-hour entry for that weekday does not contain the slot.

Users with more than one range on the same day therefore lose slots. Examples:
- A split day such as 9–12 and 13–17.
- A schedule crossing UTC midnight, which `getWorkingHours` splits into two entries (e.g. 1020–1439 on day N and 0–60 on day N+1).

A slot inside one range is always outside the other, so it is rejected. The check must instead verify that the slot lies within at least one matching range. Otherwise US-timezone organizers, and anyone with split hours, can lose most or all slots.

Slots overlapping the end of a date override are accepted

The only end-side rejection is `slotStartTime.isAfter(overrideEnd)`. Two cases slip through:
- A slot starting exactly at the override end.
- A slot that starts inside the override but ends after it, e.g. a 60-min slot starting 30 minutes before the end.

Both are considered available, so fixed hosts can still be booked outside their override window. The check should reject when `slotEndTime` is after the override end, or when `slotStartTime` is the same as or after it.

Override date matching mixes server-local and UTC calendar days

Two problems in matching an override to a slot's day:
- The override day is computed with `dayjs(date.start)...format("YYYY MM DD")`, which uses the server's local timezone, while `slotStartTime` is UTC. On non-UTC servers the dates can mismatch.
- Matching is by UTC calendar day, not by the organizer's local day the override applies to. For organizers far from UTC (e.g. PST), regular-hours slots from the previous local day that share the UTC date get evaluated against the override and wrongly rejected. Conversely, override hours on the other UTC date are not matched.

Shifted override minutes wrap around midnight and get dropped

After adding the invitee/organizer offset, start and end are converted to minute-of-day via `hour()*60+minute()`. If the shift moves an override across the invitee's midnight (e.g. 22:00–02:00 in invitee time), endTime becomes smaller than startTime and `buildSlots` discards the range. `activeOverrides` is also still filtered on the unshifted `dayjs.utc(override.start)` date, so for large offsets the override can land on the wrong invitee day. Slots on the adjacent day are then missing or incorrect.

Parsing Date.toString() output with dayjs is non-standard

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` relies on `new Date()` parsing the locale-style string from `Date.toString()` (e.g. "Tue Mar 21 2023 ... GMT+0000 (Coordinated Universal Time)"). This format is implementation-defined and drops milliseconds. Passing the Date directly, `dayjs(override.start)`, is reliable.

- Users with working hours crossing UTC midnight or split ranges.

`AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceTypeResource` returns null when the schema is not supported, for example when `realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled()` is false while the admin-permissions client still exists. The result is passed straight to `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later dereferenced via `resource.getScopes()`. In that state any group permission check that falls back to all-groups throws a NullPointerException, which surfaces as a 500. The code should return false when `resource` is null.

Group removal listener calls a V2 method that throws UnsupportedOperationException

When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled, the listener calls `management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false)` on GroupRemovedEvent. If ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is also enabled, `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2`, whose new `GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` throws UnsupportedOperationException. Deleting any group then fails. Separately, V2 has no cleanup of per-group resources (named by group id) on group deletion, so orphaned resources remain.

Wrong javadoc reference for requireManageMembers

The javadoc for `requireManageMembers` says it throws if `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false. The implementation actually checks `canManageMembers(GroupModel)`, so the reference is wrong.

The javadoc for `canManage()` says that in V2, having VIEW or MANAGE on groups grants manage. This documents the incorrect behaviour described above. Only MANAGE should grant manage.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract interface method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order()` is added as an abstract method on the public SPI interface `CryptoProvider`. Any third-party or out-of-tree implementation (custom crypto providers, older keycloak-client copies) will fail to compile. Already-compiled implementations will hit `AbstractMethodError` when `detectProvider` calls `order()`. A `default` method returning a neutral value would preserve compatibility.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations. The candidate adds details about compilation failures, AbstractMethodError, and a compatible default-method alternative.

false_positives.candidate:
Ignored providers are still instantiated and mutate global JCA state

`detectProvider` now iterates the whole `ServiceLoader` and sorts the results. That instantiates every `CryptoProvider` on the classpath, including the ones that end up ignored. These constructors have global side effects:
- `FIPS1402Provider` calls `Security.insertProviderAt` to put KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider, BCFIPS and BCJSSE at positions 1-3, and changes the ssl.KeyManagerFactory/TrustManagerFactory security properties.
- `DefaultCryptoProvider` registers BouncyCastle.

Before this change, having several providers on the classpath was a hard error, so the side effects could not go unnoticed. Now a provider that is 'ignored' (only reported in a debug log) can still reorder JVM security providers and TLS defaults. Ordering should be resolved without instantiating every provider, for example via `ServiceLoader.stream()` or a static order, or the side effects should be moved out of the constructors.

Equal-order providers now resolve silently and nondeterministically

`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return order 200. If two of them are on the classpath (e.g. FIPS plus default), selection depends on ServiceLoader iteration, which is effectively classpath order. Previously this case threw an `IllegalStateException`. Now it only logs at debug level. As a result, a deployment intended to run in FIPS mode could silently pick the non-FIPS provider. Keep failing when more than one provider shares the highest order, or give the providers distinct orders.

Test uses a P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and never verifies the re-encoded DER

The key pair is generated with the default EC size (P-256) and reused for ES384 and ES512. As a result, r and s are always about 32 bytes, and the 48- and 66-byte cases (including P-521 values with leading bytes) are never exercised. The test also only checks that DER -> RS -> DER -> RS round-trips to the same RS. It never checks that the produced DER is accepted by `Signature.verify`, or that it matches the existing BC implementation, so a symmetric encoding bug would pass. Use curve-appropriate keys (secp384r1, secp521r1) and verify the reconstructed DER signature.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test asserts before the reader thread finishes, so failures can be missed

The reader thread is started but never joined. Right after the deletes, `deletedAll` is set and `caughtExceptions` is asserted to be empty immediately. A request still in flight in the reader thread may fail and add its exception after the assertion has already passed. Exceptions are also only recorded if the thread happened to run during the deletes. The regression test can therefore pass even when the bug is present. The test should keep a reference to the thread and `join()` it (with a timeout) before asserting. Ideally it should also confirm that at least one read actually ran concurrently with the deletes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: the test sets deletedAll and asserts before waiting for the reader thread, allowing an in-flight read to record an exception after the assertion and produce a false pass.

The "advanced" branch slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. The comment claims the ORM handles negative slicing automatically, but it does not: Django raises `ValueError`/`AssertionError` ("Negative indexing is not supported").

A user-supplied cursor like `0:-5:0` therefore produces a 500 instead of a clean 400 `BadPaginationError`.

The comments also say this "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" and is "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level". That rationale is misleading. Negative offsets should be rejected, as `OffsetPaginator` does.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on Django QuerySets, which do not support negative slicing and raise an error. The candidate's additional details do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator applies math.floor/ceil to datetime keys and crashes the audit log endpoint

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` copies the integer `Paginator` implementation and runs `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `getattr(item, self.key)`.

The only caller, `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`, uses `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime`. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`.

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: get_item_key applies math.floor/ceil to a datetime key because the audit logs endpoint uses order_by="-datetime", causing a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
Raw numeric cursor value used to filter a datetime column

`value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged. `build_queryset` then emits `WHERE datetime <= %s` with that integer or float.

`DateTimePaginator` instead converts the millisecond value back into a timezone-aware `datetime`. Here the integer is compared against a timestamp column, which either raises a database error or filters incorrectly.

Any cursor-based navigation of audit logs through the optimized path is therefore broken. The paginator should extend `DateTimePaginator` (or reuse its key/value conversion) when ordering by a datetime.

BasePaginator change silently clamps negative next offsets but passes negative prev offsets to the QuerySet

This change affects every `BasePaginator` subclass (`DateTimePaginator`, `Paginator`, etc.) used across the API.

- For forward cursors, a negative offset is now silently clamped to 0. But `build_cursor` still computes the next cursor from the original negative `cursor.offset`, so the returned next/prev cursors can be wrong (e.g. `offset + limit` stays negative or small).
- For `is_prev` cursors, the negative offset is still passed straight into `queryset[offset:stop]`, which errors.

The comment calling this "safe" is incorrect. Malformed cursors should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` rather than half-handled.

New paginator and endpoint branch have no tests

The PR adds a new paginator, a new query parameter (`optimized_pagination`), and changes the core `BasePaginator.get_result` offset handling, all without tests.

A basic test of `optimized_pagination=true` for an org owner returning audit rows would have exposed the `TypeError` on datetime keys. A test with a negative-offset cursor would have exposed the unsupported negative slice.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same key

With the coarse lock gone, nothing stops two callers from building the same NamespacedResource at once. Callers include `getOrCreateIndex` from Search (including federated lookups) and from `handleEvent`, and the init workers. Each caller sees `GetIndex == nil` and calls `BuildIndex`.

For in-memory indexes, one fully built index silently replaces the other. Writes applied to the losing index by a concurrent watch event are lost, and the IndexTenants/IndexedKinds metrics are double counted.

For file-based indexes (`size > FileThreshold`), both callers run `bleve.New` on the same directory and the second fails. A per-key singleflight or lock is needed to keep the speedup without this race.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race: removing the coarse BuildIndex lock permits multiple goroutines to concurrently build an index for the same key. Its additional consequences and suggested per-key synchronization do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates cache map without lock while builds can now write it concurrently

`BuildIndex` no longer holds `cacheMu` for its whole body; it now writes `b.cache[key]` under a short lock. `TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` without taking `cacheMu` at all.

In `searchSupport.init`, the watch goroutine is started (search.go:207) before `s.search.TotalDocs()` is called (search.go:216). `handleEvent` -> `getOrCreateIndex` -> `BuildIndex` can therefore write the map while `TotalDocs` is iterating it. Search requests can do the same once the server is up.

Concurrent map iteration and write is a fatal runtime error in Go and will crash the process. `TotalDocs` should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unsynchronized iteration of b.cache in TotalDocs racing with BuildIndex writes triggered by the watcher started before the call, potentially causing a concurrent map iteration/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Init worker goroutines race on shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed`

Inside `group.Go`, each goroutine assigns the outer `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` with no synchronization. Both are data races.

This PR's goal is to make these builds actually run in parallel by removing the backend lock, which makes the races far more likely to bite. One goroutine's error can be overwritten by another, and the reported count is unreliable.

The goroutine should use a local `err` and an atomic counter.

Requests are no longer rejected after Stop

`Stop` still sets `s.initErr` to "service is stopping" / "service is stopped". Previously every handler called `s.Init(ctx)`, which returned that `initErr`, so requests were rejected after shutdown.

This PR removes those `Init` calls from all handlers. After `Stop`, Create/Read/List/Watch/etc. now run against a stopped backend instead of returning a clean error. `initErr` is effectively dead after construction.

Either keep a cheap stopped/initErr check in the handlers or remove the now-meaningless assignments.

Context cancel leaked when Init fails in constructor

`NewResourceServer` creates `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` and then returns `nil, err` if `s.Init(ctx)` fails, without calling `cancel`.

Any goroutines or watchers started during partial initialization keep running. For example, the search watch goroutine may already be started if only `initWatcher` failed. They are never cancelled.

`cancel()` should be called on the error path.

Postgres integration test skipped instead of fixed

The storage-server module test is now skipped for postgres in CI. This likely follows from the behaviour change to eager initialization in the constructor, which is exactly what the test exercises.

Skipping it removes coverage for eager init against postgres, the scenario the PR description itself asks reviewers to worry about. It should be fixed, or the root cause should be documented.

true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that the test's no-commit assertion contradicts its docstring stating that errors should not block commits, matching the golden concern about the docstring not matching the implementation. The additional timing/flakiness claim does not negate that match.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared FixedQueuePool is permanently shut down on first rebalance, silently dropping messages afterwards

The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory `__init__`. Every strategy from `create_with_partitions` reuses it, but `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down all queues and stops the workers.

Arroyo closes the strategy on every partition revocation, so after the first rebalance the next strategy gets a dead pool. `work_queue.put` then raises `queue.ShutDown`. `submit` catches it and marks the offset as completed. As a result every subsequent message is skipped without being processed, yet its offset is committed. This is silent data loss.

The pool should be owned by the strategy (created per `create_with_partitions`), or the strategy should not shut down a factory-owned pool.

Arroyo commit callback invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `commit_function` there, which invokes the Arroyo `Commit` callable. That callable stages offsets on the `StreamProcessor`/`KafkaConsumer`, which are single-threaded and not thread-safe. This races with `poll`/`stage_offsets` on the main thread.

It can also commit offsets for partitions that were already revoked, because the commit thread and workers keep running during a rebalance. Offsets should be collected in the background but committed from the strategy's `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread.

Unbounded queues: no backpressure despite docstring claim

Each `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. A slow group therefore lets its queue grow without limit while the consumer keeps polling Kafka, so memory grows unbounded.

The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which is false. Bound the queues and reject or pause when they are full.

Commits stall permanently on natural Kafka offset gaps

`get_committable_offsets` stops at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous: transactional control markers and compacted topics both leave gaps. Any such gap means the committed offset never advances past it, even though every received message is processed.

The result is ever-growing reported lag and full reprocessing on restart. The contiguity check should only consider offsets that were actually received, for example by advancing to the minimum outstanding offset minus 1, or to the max seen when nothing is outstanding.

close() stops committing before workers drain, so processed work is never committed

`close()` first sets `shutdown_event` and joins the commit thread. Only after that does it shut down the pool, which lets workers finish their remaining queued items. There is no final commit.

Items completed during that drain, plus anything completed in the last second before shutdown, are never committed. They get reprocessed after every rebalance or restart. Drain the workers first, then perform one final commit.

The previous code wrapped the unified-storage result in `updateWrapper`, so legacy received exactly the object written to unified storage. Now the raw `objInfo` is replayed in a goroutine, and the update or patch is applied to whatever old object legacy holds. For PATCH/apply, or when the stores already differ, legacy ends up with different content than unified storage. Reusing `objInfo` concurrently after the request has finished is also unsafe.

Request object shared with a background goroutine while the handler keeps using it

`obj` and `options` are passed to `d.Legacy.Create` in a goroutine after the method has already returned `created`, which may be the same pointer or derived from `obj`. The apiserver goes on encoding or mutating the response while legacy storage reads or mutates the same object, which is a data race. The object should be deep-copied before handing it to the goroutine.

Unit tests never verify the async legacy write and race with it

The tests return right after the dual-writer call without waiting for the background goroutine, so nothing asserts that the legacy write happens. Legacy and storage mocks share a single `mock.Mock`, so expectations meant for one store satisfy calls to the other. For example, the 'unified store fails' Create case only fails because the legacy expectation for `failingObj` is matched by the storage call. A goroutine can also invoke the mock after the subtest finishes.

Mode 3 integration tests check legacy reads immediately after async writes

`doPlaylistTests` creates or updates through k8s and then immediately queries the legacy `/api/playlists` endpoints via `getFromBothAPIs` and the search check. In mode 3 the legacy write is asynchronous, so these assertions race the background goroutine. If the legacy endpoint reads legacy storage, the test will be flaky; if it reads unified storage, legacy consistency is not being tested at all.

With the accelerator patch, translations load on demand. `I18n.translate` only loads `config.locale`, and the fallback locales (site default and `:en`) are loaded only by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`. The fallback locales should be loaded inside `I18n.translate`/`load_locale`, not in a controller filter.

Two problems follow. (1) If the site's default locale changes, cached fallback strings from the old default locale keep being served until the process restarts or the entry is evicted. (2) If a key is translated before the fallback locales are loaded (e.g. outside a controller), the 'translation missing' result is frozen into the cache. It is then returned even after the fallback locales are loaded. The cache key should include the fallback chain, or the cache should be cleared when the default locale changes.

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds a new array and reads `SiteSetting.default_locale` on every call. The Fallbacks backend calls it on every uncached translate, which includes every translate call that has interpolation or count arguments, since those bypass the LRU cache. This allocates a new array on every one of those calls and adds avoidable overhead to a very hot path.

The PR changes translation resolution for every locale but adds no specs. Untested cases include: fallback to the site locale then to English, loading of the fallback locales, and behavior in non-request contexts. Regressions such as the missing-load issue in jobs would go unnoticed.
